The document is an APA-format author manuscript watermarked 'UNDER PEER REVIEW' and prints no date. It is not the version of record: the ACM Creativity & Cognition 2026 paper (doi:10.1145/3803784.3816857, published 2026-07-13) returned HTTP 403, so its body text, sample, and statistics were not compared.
source.title_on_document: The role of human agency in human-AI co-creativity

supplement.where: Appendix A (Experimental Platform and Paradigm, pp. 33-37) and Appendix B (Additional Results, pp. 38-42) are bound into this PDF. No separate online supplement is referenced. The OSF preregistration is linked on p. 10.
supplement.holds: Table A2 (p. 35): mixed-model coefficients and SEs for creativity, originality, and usefulness. Table A3 (p. 36): mixed-model coefficients and SEs for cosine similarity to the condition-object centroid. Also Figure A1 condition instructions (p. 33), Table A1 rubric (p. 34), participant-AI similarity (p. 37), and noncompliance, prompt coding, and chat-behavior tests (pp. 38-42). The main text prints no coefficient table.

paper_design_summary: Community college students in the San Francisco Bay Area (submitters) were randomly assigned to high-agency instructions with access to a gpt-3.5 chatbot, low-agency instructions ('AI does the heavy lifting') with the same chatbot, or a human-only control told not to use AI. Each submitter wrote five alternative uses for each of three objects (brick, bubble wrap, frisbee). Separate online evaluators rated ideas for creativity, originality, and usefulness, and the authors measured homogeneity by embedding similarity to a leave-one-out condition-object centroid (preregistered) and by HDBSCAN cluster metrics (exploratory).

studies.label: Single experiment: agency instructions with AI access, or no AI, on the Alternative Uses Task

assignment.what_was_assigned: Condition: high-agency instructions with chatbot access, low-agency instructions with chatbot access, or human-only control without AI (Figure A1, p. 33)
assignment.quote: After consenting, participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions that varied whether they completed the idea-generation task with or without access to an AI chatbot
assignment.locator: p. 11, Method, Submission Phase; Figure A1, p. 33
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 10, Method, Preregistration (https://osf.io/2d7fe/overview?view_only=c34f80bd046e4c85aafdee3d2c33a74e); deviations listed p. 14, Statistical Approach

arms.name: High-Agency
arms.description: Access to the embedded gpt-3.5 chatbot. Instruction (Figure A1, p. 33): 'Instead of asking AI to come up with ideas for you, use it to expand upon your own ideas to generate ones that are even more creative.'

arms.name: Low-Agency
arms.description: Access to the same chatbot. Instruction (Figure A1, p. 33): 'Let the AI's creative power work for you. Trust in its ability to generate creative ideas and don't hesitate to use its suggestions directly.' The text adds: 'The beauty of AI is that it does the heavy lifting for you' (p. 11).

arms.name: Control (human only)
arms.description: Same AUT with no chatbot. Instruction: 'We value your individual human creativity, so please do NOT use AI during the task.' Copy-paste was disabled (p. 11; Figure A1, p. 33).

participants.exclusions: The paper reports N = 150 submitters (p. 10), called the 'final sample' (p. 14), and adds: 'An additional three submitters were excluded for failing an initial attention check' (p. 10). The paper gives no count at assignment. All 150 were assigned and produced ideas (2,250 ideas, five for each of three objects, pp. 12 and 14), but the paper does not say whether the three excluded submitters had been assigned, and it reports no other attrition, so the number randomized is not known. Object trials from the two AI arms were dropped if they had no chat data. Participants did not use the AI tool in 24 percent of all low-agency trials and 38 percent of all high-agency trials (p. 13). This exclusion removed 22 people entirely (12 high-agency, 10 low-agency, 'completely excluded from the analysis', pp. 13-14), leaving 128 people analyzed by subtraction (150 - 22). It also removed some trials of the AI-arm participants who stayed. The paper prints neither 128, nor any per-arm count, nor the share of trials that the remaining participants lost. Ideas never drawn for evaluation are excluded from the rating models (p. 13). The analysis is per-protocol, not intention-to-treat. The preregistered target was N = 450 (p. 14). Evaluators are a separate rater sample (N = 142, CloudResearch Connect). The sentence after their description reads: 'Six participants were excluded for failing an initial attention check and five participants were excluded due to idea data logging issues' (p. 10). It names no sample. Its placement suggests evaluators, most clearly for the six, because the submitter attention-check exclusions are given separately as three, but that is a reading, not a statement. The text does not say whether 142 is before or after these exclusions.
participants.who: Community college students in the San Francisco Bay Area participating for research credits (Research Experience Program, p. 22); age M = 25.1 (SD = 9.2); 72 percent female. Ratings came from a separate sample of U.S. adults on CloudResearch Connect (N = 142; age M = 46.7, SD = 16.3).
participants.quote: Submitters were community college students in the San Francisco Bay Area (N = 150; age: M = 25.1 years, SD = 9.2; 72% female, 24% male, 1.3% non-binary, 2.7% self-described) who participated for research credits.
participants.locator: p. 10, Participants; p. 12, Occasions; pp. 13-14, Manipulation Checks; p. 14, Data Structure and Statistical Approach

ai_tool.name_model: Custom chatbot web app (Vercel) built on gpt-3.5, temperature 0.7, generic helpful-assistant system prompt, embedded in the Qualtrics survey (p. 11; Appendix A, p. 33)
ai_tool.how_used: Participants in both AI arms could chat freely with the embedded chatbot, one conversation per object, and typed their five uses per object in fields below it. The arms differed only in the agency instructions shown before the task (p. 12; p. 14; Figure A1, p. 33).

task.description: Alternative Uses Task: five non-standard uses for each of three objects (bubble wrap, frisbee, brick), object order counterbalanced; 2,250 ideas in total (p. 12)
task.duration: One session, average completion time 30 minutes; no time limit (p. 12)

outcomes.name: Overall creativity rated by evaluators
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: U.S. adults on CloudResearch Connect (N = 142) each rated a random subset of 15 ideas, five per object, on overall creativity, originality, and usefulness, using the Table A1 rubric (p. 13; p. 34). The text does not state the evaluators' rating scale (submitters' self-ratings used 1 = Not at all to 5 = Maximally, p. 12; Figure 1 axes run 1 to 5, p. 30). Linear mixed model (lme4) with condition as fixed effect and random intercepts for submitters and objects; Low-Agency is the reference level (Table A2, p. 35). Ideas never drawn for evaluation are excluded (p. 13). Submitters' self-ratings are self-report and are not listed.

outcomes.name: Homogeneity: cosine similarity of each idea to the leave-one-out condition-object centroid
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: One randomly sampled idea per participant per object; all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings; cosine similarity to the leave-one-out centroid of the other ideas in the same condition and object. Higher similarity means more homogeneous, so the directions below are coded on diversity (sign reversed). Linear mixed model with condition as fixed effect and random intercepts for participants and objects; Tukey HSD pairwise tests. The p. 15 formula reads 1 - cosine, but Table A3, Figure 2, and p. 16 report cosine similarity.

contrasts.reported: Table A3 (reference Low-Agency; outcome cosine similarity to centroid): (Intercept) 0.441*** (0.015); Control -0.014 (0.019), no star; Num.Obs. 337. No Tukey test for this pair is printed; the text says low-agency and control participants 'produced ideas that were similarly homogeneous'. Direction coded on diversity (similarity sign reversed).
contrasts.locator: p. 36, Table A3; p. 16, Results, Homogeneity; p. 31, Figure 2

contrasts.reported: Tukey HSD: 'no differences in idea homogeneity between the high-agency condition and the control condition, t(122) = 1.87, p = .15'. No High-Agency vs Control coefficient printed; Table A3 gives High-Agency -0.050* (0.021) and Control -0.014 (0.019), both relative to Low-Agency.
contrasts.locator: p. 16, Results, Homogeneity; p. 36, Table A3; p. 31, Figure 2

contrasts.reported: Table A3 (reference Low-Agency): High-Agency -0.050* (0.021) in cosine similarity; (Intercept) 0.441*** (0.015). Tukey HSD: high-agency ideas were 'less similar to the condition-object centroid' than low-agency ideas, t(125) = -2.45, p < .05. Direction coded on diversity: high-agency ideas less similar, so more diverse.
contrasts.locator: p. 36, Table A3; p. 16, Results, Homogeneity; p. 31, Figure 2

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity of an idea's embedding to the leave-one-out centroid of the other ideas in the same condition and object (higher = more homogeneous). The p. 15 text writes the score as 1 - cosine(idea embedding, centroid embedding), but Table A3, Figure 2, and the p. 16 text report and interpret cosine similarity.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each sampled idea against the leave-one-out centroid, 'the average embedding of all ideas other than the one being compared', within its condition and object (p. 15). One randomly sampled idea per participant per object enters the model. The text does not say whether the centroid averages all submitted ideas or only the sampled ones.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Linear mixed model (lme4) on output-level scores with random intercepts for submitters and objects (Table A3); Tukey HSD pairwise comparisons; Figure 2 shows bootstrapped 95 percent CIs of condition means
diversity_detail.notes: Preregistered H2 outcome. Omnibus condition effect: F(2, 121.67) = 3.15, p < .05, partial eta squared = .07 (p. 16); this is the three-condition test, not a single contrast. Figure 2 (p. 31) plots condition means with bootstrapped 95 percent CIs but prints no numeric values. No arm means or SDs are printed.

outcomes.name: Number of unique HDBSCAN clusters (exploratory)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: HDBSCAN on sentence embeddings, run for each object-condition combination; minimum cluster size 6, minimum samples 1, cluster selection epsilon 0.25 (p. 17). The number of unique clusters is a proxy for the number of unique categories of uses; more clusters = more diverse.

contrasts.reported: Permutation test (n = 5,000 permutations) comparing the maximum and minimum condition means; the statistic is the observed difference: 'the observed difference between conditions was 3.33, a difference driven by the statistically higher number of clusters in the control condition relative to the low-agency condition, p = .04'. Per-condition counts not printed. Direction coded on diversity.

diversity_detail.embedding_model: Sentence embeddings; the clustering paragraphs name no model (the Analytic Approach names all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for the homogeneity analysis, p. 14)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Ideas in each of the nine condition-object combinations (Figure 3). The paper does not say whether all submitted ideas or only the one sampled idea per participant entered the clustering.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Permutation test with 5,000 permutations comparing the maximum and minimum condition means; only that pair is tested
diversity_detail.notes: Exploratory. High-Agency values appear only in the Figure 3 t-SNE plots, with no numbers.

outcomes.name: Noise ratio: share of ideas not assigned to any HDBSCAN cluster (exploratory)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Proportion of ideas HDBSCAN labels as noise, read by the authors as a proxy for 'outlier' ideas indicative of greater diversity (p. 17); higher = more diverse. Same clustering settings as S1-O5.

contrasts.reported: Permutation test (5,000 permutations; the statistic is the observed difference between the maximum and minimum condition means): 'For noise ratio, the observed difference was 0.22, again driven by a higher noise ratio in the control condition relative to the low-agency, condition p = .02.' Per-condition values not printed. Direction coded on diversity.

diversity_detail.metric: HDBSCAN noise ratio (share of ideas not assigned to any cluster)
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Sentence embeddings; the clustering paragraphs name no model (the Analytic Approach names all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for the homogeneity analysis, p. 14)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Ideas in each of the nine condition-object combinations (Figure 3). The paper does not say whether all submitted ideas or only the one sampled idea per participant entered the clustering.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Permutation test with 5,000 permutations comparing the maximum and minimum condition means; only that pair is tested

outcomes.name: Coefficient of variation of HDBSCAN cluster sizes (exploratory)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Standard deviation of cluster sizes divided by mean cluster size (p. 17). A higher CV means more imbalance in cluster sizes, which the authors read as participants converging on one category, so higher = less diverse. Same clustering settings as S1-O5.

contrasts.reported: Permutation test (5,000 permutations; the statistic is the observed difference between the maximum and minimum condition means): 'For coefficient of variation, the observed difference was 0.75, driven by the low-agency condition having a significantly higher coefficient of variation than the control condition, p = .005.' Per-condition values not printed. Direction coded on diversity (higher CV = less diverse).
contrasts.locator: p. 17, Results, Homogeneity; p. 18, Discussion; p. 32, Figure 3

diversity_detail.metric: Coefficient of variation of cluster sizes
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Sentence embeddings; the clustering paragraphs name no model (the Analytic Approach names all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for the homogeneity analysis, p. 14)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Cluster sizes within each of the nine condition-object combinations (Figure 3). The paper does not say whether all submitted ideas or only the one sampled idea per participant entered the clustering.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Permutation test with 5,000 permutations comparing the maximum and minimum condition means; only that pair is tested
diversity_detail.notes: Exploratory. The Discussion (p. 18) says the low-agency CV was significantly greater than both the high-agency and control conditions, but the Results (p. 17) report only the maximum-minimum test (low-agency vs control).

company_involvement.description: Five of the seven authors list BetterUp Labs (affiliation 3): A. Y. Lee, A. Liebscher, K. Rapuano, K. G. Niederhoffer, and J. T. Hancock. Authors with BetterUp affiliations are paid employees of BetterUp Inc., and Lee and Hancock are paid consultants within BetterUp Labs. Wu and Yang declare no BetterUp affiliation. Yang implemented the chatbot, a custom web app on gpt-3.5 that the authors built, and the paper names no BetterUp product. The document has no funding statement.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, affiliations; p. 22, Contributions and Competing Interests; p. 33, Appendix A

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to one of two arms with access to the same gpt-3.5 chatbot and different agency instructions, or to a no-AI control (p. 11). The final sample is N = 150 submitters (pp. 10, 14). After 22 AI-arm noncompliers were completely excluded (pp. 13-14), 128 people were analyzed by subtraction, well above 50. The paper prints neither the analyzed nor the per-arm counts, but Table A3's 337 observations, one sampled idea per participant per object, need at least 113 people (p. 15; p. 36). Outcomes are third-party evaluator ratings of the submitted ideas and embedding and cluster measures of homogeneity across those ideas, produced while the AI arms had the chatbot available (pp. 12-13, 15-17). Caveats: the analysis is per-protocol, and the authors write that noncompliance 'somewhat compromised the random assignment' (p. 20), which bears on the AI-vs-control contrasts. The sample is a third of the preregistered 450 (p. 14). The setting (supervised or remote) is not stated, so design_class online_rct is provisional; lab_rct would also be core.

one_line_finding: Evaluator ratings of creativity and originality did not differ significantly by condition (ps > .60, p. 15; Table A2, p. 35), high-agency ideas were less similar to their condition-object centroid than low-agency ideas (cosine similarity -0.050, SE 0.021, Table A3, p. 36; Tukey t(125) = -2.45, p < .05, p. 16), and low-agency ideas formed fewer clusters, had a lower noise ratio, and had more unequal cluster sizes than control ideas (permutation p = .04, .02, and .005, p. 17).
open_questions: Analyzed and per-arm counts are never printed: 128 analyzed is 150 minus the 22 complete exclusions, and Table A3's 337 observations (one sampled idea per participant per object) need at least 113 people. The Tukey tests (t(125), t(122), p. 16) and the Appendix B t-tests (t(79), pp. 41-42) report degrees of freedom, not counts of people. The share of trials lost by the AI-arm participants who stayed is not printed either.

Number randomized: the paper gives no count at assignment. All 150 submitters in the final sample were assigned, but the paper does not say whether the three submitters excluded for an 'initial attention check' (p. 10) had been assigned, and it reports no other attrition, so the count at assignment has a floor of 150 and no stated ceiling. The ACM version of record, the OSF preregistration, or the authors may settle it.

Five 'idea data logging' exclusions: the p. 10 sentence after the evaluator description calls them 'participants' and names no sample. Placement suggests evaluators. If they were submitters, the counts at assignment or analysis would differ, but criterion 2 holds under any reading.

Usefulness, Low-Agency vs Control: the Results say low-agency ideas were 'significantly more useful, β = 0.20, p = .04' (p. 15) without naming the comparison group, and no Table A2 coefficient equals 0.20. Table A2 shows Control -0.162 (0.090) relative to Low-Agency with no star (p. 35), and the abstract (p. 2) and Discussion (p. 17) say usefulness did not differ. The direction is now no_clear_difference, following those three sources. The p. 15 sentence stays in 'reported' as an unexplained conflict.

Creativity and originality: the text reports 'ps > .60' for the treatment conditions relative to control (p. 15) without naming the test, but Table A2's Control coefficients relative to Low-Agency (-0.082, SE 0.081; -0.077, SE 0.098) are about one standard error from zero, which does not fit p > .60 for that pair. The direction is no_clear_difference under either reading, and extraction should use Table A2.

Homogeneity metric: p. 15 writes the score as 1 - cosine(idea embedding, centroid embedding), yet Table A3, Figure 2, and p. 16 report and interpret cosine similarity (higher = more homogeneous). Coded here as similarity.
Figure 1's note (p. 30) describes cosine similarity scores although the panels show creativity, originality, and usefulness ratings; it appears copied from Figure 2.

Clustering inputs: the paper does not say which ideas entered HDBSCAN (all submitted ideas or one sampled idea per participant) or which embedding model the clustering used (pp. 16-17, p. 32). The centroid analysis does not say whether the leave-one-out centroid averages all submitted ideas or only the sampled ones (p. 15).

Setting: the paper does not say whether submitters completed the Qualtrics session remotely or in a supervised lab. They were community college students taking part for research credits through the Research Experience Program (pp. 10, 22), a student pool rather than an online panel. design_class online_rct is a provisional reading of the p. 11 control instruction, which cites AI use by online survey respondents in past work. If the session was supervised, lab_rct applies. Both codes are core, so criterion 1 does not change.

Primary record: both AI arms used the same open chatbot and differ only in instructions, so neither is plain, uninstructed chatbot use. The low-agency arm ('let AI do the work') may be closer to default use.
Version: the ACM Creativity & Cognition 2026 version of record was not retrieved and may report the sample or statistics differently.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are self-reports or do not measure creativity or across-people diversity: submitters' self-ratings of one own idea per object (creativity, originality, value, perceived uniqueness; p. 12); self-reported AI helpfulness, AI as a conversational partner, and intrinsic motivation (pp. 12-13); participant-AI semantic similarity between submitted ideas and the AI's suggestions (high vs low agency, ps > .05; p. 37); prompt-type classification (Direct Ask: Low-Agency M = 0.84, SD = 0.29 vs High-Agency M = 0.50, SD = 0.45, t(79) = 4.01, p < .001, d = 0.91; Exploratory: High-Agency M = 0.46, SD = 0.44 vs Low-Agency M = 0.15, SD = 0.26, t(79) = 3.81, p < .001, d = 0.86; pp. 41-42); chat-log behaviors (turns, duration, words per turn, copy-paste events), ps > .17 (p. 38). No fluency outcome: every submitter was asked for exactly five ideas per object, although the abstract mentions ideational fluency (p. 2). Each rating model has 1,709 observations (Table A2), and each evaluator rated 15 ideas on three dimensions (p. 13). Low-Agency, not the control, is the reference level in Tables A2 and A3. Noncompliance: no AI use in 24 percent of low-agency and 38 percent of high-agency trials (pp. 13, 39), mostly refusals on principle according to participant feedback (p. 39).

differences.resolved: null (unresolved). The paper never gives a count at assignment. N = 150 is the submitter sample after three exclusions for an 'initial attention check' (p. 10), which p. 14 calls the 'final sample', and the 22 later exclusions come out of it. The paper does not say whether the attention check came before or after random assignment, so 150 (check before) or 153 (check after) people were randomized. Missing: the timing of the attention check relative to assignment, or a printed count at assignment (possibly in the ACM version of record or the OSF preregistration). The form keeps null and states 150 in participants.exclusions.

differences.resolved: yes. In both AI arms the chatbot sat above the answer fields while participants typed their ideas, and AI-arm trials without chat data were dropped, so every analyzed AI-arm idea was produced with AI available. The control arm's lack of AI is the comparison in every with_ai contrast, not a mix within the outcome. The codebook sets outcome_with_ai to true when AI was available while the scored output was produced, and both forms already code these outcomes with_ai and across_people on that basis.

differences.resolved: Neither form exactly. One randomly sampled idea per participant per object is compared with a leave-one-out centroid that the paper defines as the average embedding of all other ideas in the same condition and object. The paper does not say whether that centroid averages all submitted ideas or only the sampled ones, so form A's 'sampled' is not stated.
differences.quote: The centroid embedding used a leave-one-out approach: the average embedding of all ideas other than the one being compared.

differences.a: All ideas in each condition-object set, with a note that the paper does not state whether all five ideas per participant or one sampled idea entered
differences.b: All submitted ideas in each condition-object pool
differences.resolved: Ideas in each of the nine condition-object combinations; the paper does not say whether all submitted ideas or only the one sampled idea per participant entered the clustering (form A's caveat). Neither the clustering paragraphs nor the Figure 3 note name the idea sample.
differences.quote: Clusters were identified for each combination of object and condition using HDBSCAN and visualized in 2D using t-SNE.
differences.locator: p. 32, Figure 3 note; pp. 16-17, Results, Homogeneity

differences.a: Four authors list BetterUp Labs affiliation; employees and consultants as declared; funding source not stated
differences.b: Liebscher, Rapuano, and Niederhoffer affiliated with BetterUp Labs; Lee and Hancock paid consultants; BetterUp did not build the AI tool
differences.resolved: Five of the seven authors list BetterUp Labs (affiliation 3): Lee, Liebscher, Rapuano, Niederhoffer, and Hancock, so form A's count of four is wrong. BetterUp-affiliated authors are paid employees of BetterUp Inc., and Lee and Hancock are paid consultants within BetterUp Labs. Form B's claim that BetterUp did not build the tool is not stated: the authors ('we') built the web app on gpt-3.5, Yang (no BetterUp affiliation) implemented it, and the paper names no BetterUp product. No funding statement appears.
differences.quote: Authors with BetterUp affiliations are paid employees of BetterUp Inc.; A. Lee and J. Hancock are paid consultants within BetterUp Labs at BetterUp, Inc.

open_items.item: Analyzed and per-arm counts of people, and the trials kept per arm, are not printed (128 analyzed by subtraction; Table A3 needs at least 113 people). Extraction needs them for n_treatment and n_control. If the version of record does not print them, the authors can.

Number randomized (also the unresolved reconciliation difference on participants.n_randomized): no count at assignment is given, the timing of the attention check is not stated, and no other attrition is reported. Criterion 2 counts people analyzed, which exceed 50 under any reading. Fallbacks: the OSF preregistration or the authors.
Sample of the five 'idea data logging' exclusions is not named (placement suggests evaluators). Criterion 2 holds under any reading.

Usefulness, Low-Agency vs Control: the p. 15 'β = 0.20, p = .04' names no comparison group and matches no Table A2 coefficient. It is coded no_clear_difference from Table A2, the abstract, and the Discussion. This is a conflict in the results, not in eligibility. Fallback: the authors.

Creativity and originality: 'ps > .60' (p. 15) does not fit Table A2's Low-Agency vs Control coefficients, which are about one SE from zero. The direction is no_clear_difference under either reading, and extraction uses Table A2.
Homogeneity formula: p. 15 writes 1 - cosine, but Table A3, Figure 2, and p. 16 report cosine similarity. Coded as similarity, with the sign reversed for diversity.
Figure 1's note describes cosine similarity scores, but the panels show ratings (the note appears copied from Figure 2).

Clustering and centroid inputs: the paper does not say which ideas entered HDBSCAN and the leave-one-out centroid (all submitted ideas or only the sampled ones), or which embedding model the clustering used. This matters for comparing diversity effects, not for eligibility. Fallback: the authors.
Setting (remote or supervised) is not stated. design_class online_rct is provisional, and lab_rct applies if the session was supervised. Both codes are core.

Primary record: both AI arms got agency instructions, so neither is uninstructed chatbot use, and the low-agency arm may be closer to default use. This is a coding choice for the extraction phase under codebook section 8, rule 3.

Version: the form rests on the PsyArXiv preprint. The ACM Creativity & Cognition 2026 version of record (HTTP 403) was not compared, and the codebook takes the latest version as the paper. It reports the same experiment with the same abstract, so eligibility is not expected to change, but every number should be checked against it.
